## MPPSC Assistant Professor 2026: where this recruitment stands

MPPSC Assistant Professor 2026 is a recruitment of 949 posts in Madhya Pradesh government colleges and state universities, conducted by the Madhya Pradesh Public Service Commission. Applications have closed, and the exam stage is under way: admit cards for the next batch of subjects were released on 29 July 2026 on mppsc.mp.gov.in, with those exams on 30 August 2026.

The thing that confuses almost everyone searching for this recruitment is that the dates appear to contradict each other. One page says the exam was on 12 July 2026, another says 30 August 2026, a third gives an application deadline that has already passed. All of them can be right at once.

MPPSC is not running this as one exam. It is running it as a series of subject groups, each with its own application window, its own admit card release, and its own exam date. Your dates depend entirely on which subject you applied for. Checking a date meant for a different subject group is the single most common mistake candidates make here.

## Exam schedule by subject group

These are the batches confirmed so far. Check the one that matches your subject, and confirm on mppsc.mp.gov.in, since MPPSC has issued corrigenda revising dates more than once in this recruitment.

| Subject group | Admit card | Exam date |
|---|---|---|
| Sanskrit, Geography, Psychology, Law, Geology, Yogic Science | 2 July 2026 | 12 July 2026, at Indore |
| History, Physics, Chemistry, Botany, Mathematics and the subjects grouped with them | 29 July 2026 | 30 August 2026 |

A corrigendum dated 25 June 2026 revised the schedule for History, Physics, Chemistry, Botany and Mathematics, which is why older pages carry different dates for those subjects. If your subject is not listed above, MPPSC publishes the schedule group by group, so watch the commission's notice board rather than relying on aggregator pages.

## Application window, and the late fee structure

Applications are closed. The revised last date to apply online was 9 June 2026, and MPPSC then ran an unusual two-tier late window: applications with a late fee of Rs 3,000 were accepted from 10 to 16 June 2026, and applications with an ultra-late fee of Rs 25,000 were accepted on 17 June 2026.

That Rs 25,000 figure is not a misprint, and it is worth knowing about for the next cycle. MPPSC uses steep late fees rather than simply closing the window, which means a candidate who misses the ordinary deadline still has a route in, at a price that for most people is several months of the salary they are applying for. Apply inside the ordinary window.

The ordinary application fee was Rs 540 for General candidates and candidates from outside Madhya Pradesh, and Rs 290 for SC, ST, OBC and EWS candidates who are residents of Madhya Pradesh.

## Vacancy breakdown

The 949 posts span Arts, Commerce, Social Sciences and Science subjects. The largest allocations reported are as follows.

| Subject | Posts |
|---|---|
| Chemistry | 160 |
| Physics | 145 |
| Commerce | 94 |
| Economics | 84 |
| Geography | 74 |

The remaining posts are distributed across the other subjects, including History, Mathematics, Botany, Zoology, Sanskrit, Psychology, Law, Geology and Yogic Science. Category reservation applies within each subject as per Madhya Pradesh government rules, covering General, SC, ST, OBC and EWS.

Two things follow from that table. Chemistry and Physics together account for over 300 of the 949 posts, so science candidates face a much wider opening than those in smaller subjects. And because reservation is applied within each subject, your real competition is the pool in your subject and category, not the headline figure of 949.

## Eligibility

On education, you need a Master's degree in the relevant subject with at least 55 per cent marks, or an equivalent grade, from a recognised university. Candidates in reserved categories get the usual relaxation to 50 per cent as per UGC norms.

On the eligibility test, you need to have qualified the National Eligibility Test conducted by UGC, or CSIR NET, or the State Level Eligibility Test or State Eligibility Test, including the Madhya Pradesh SLET. Candidates holding a PhD awarded in accordance with the UGC regulations are exempt from the NET requirement.

That exemption is worth reading carefully, because it is conditional rather than automatic. The PhD must have been awarded in compliance with the UGC Regulations on minimum standards and procedure for the award of the degree, which set requirements on coursework, evaluation and viva. A PhD that does not meet those conditions does not carry the exemption, and this is checked at document verification rather than at the application stage.

On age, the band is 21 to 40 years, with relaxation for reserved categories and other specified groups as per Madhya Pradesh rules. The reckoning date is set in the advertisement.

## Exam pattern

The exam is offline and OMR based, with two papers on the same day in separate sessions.

| Paper | Content | Session | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paper 1 | General Studies | 10:00 am to 11:00 am | 1 hour |
| Paper 2 | Subject specific | 1:00 pm to 4:00 pm | 3 hours |

The structure tells you where the weight sits. Paper 2 runs three times as long as Paper 1, and it is the paper that tests your actual discipline at postgraduate level. Paper 1 is a general studies qualifying-style paper covering the areas common to Madhya Pradesh state exams.

Candidates who come from a research background often make the opposite mistake to the one you would expect: they prepare Paper 2 thoroughly, which they would pass anyway, and neglect Paper 1, which covers material they have not touched since their own competitive exam years.

## Paper 1: what General Studies covers

Paper 1 draws on the standard Madhya Pradesh state exam general studies base: Indian history with emphasis on the freedom movement, Indian and Madhya Pradesh geography, Indian polity and the Constitution, the Indian and state economy, general science and technology, current affairs at national and state level, and Madhya Pradesh specific general knowledge covering the state's districts, rivers, tribes, festivals, historical sites and current schemes.

Higher education policy topics appear as well, including the National Education Policy, UGC regulations, and the structure of higher education administration in the state, which are directly relevant to the post being filled.

For a candidate with a research background and no recent state-exam preparation, this paper needs deliberate work over a few weeks. It is a single hour of the day, but it is the part of the exam where the marginal marks are easiest to gain.

## Paper 2: the subject paper

Paper 2 tests your subject at the level expected of someone about to teach it in an undergraduate and postgraduate setting. In practice the syllabus tracks the UGC NET syllabus for the subject fairly closely, extended in places to reflect the Madhya Pradesh university curriculum.

The most efficient preparation is to work from your own postgraduate syllabus and the UGC NET syllabus for the subject together, since between them they cover almost everything MPPSC asks. Past MPPSC papers for your subject, where available, tell you which areas the commission favours, and those preferences tend to persist across cycles.

## Salary and what the post actually pays

The post is placed at Academic Level 10 of the 7th Pay Commission structure for teachers, with a pay range of Rs 57,700 to Rs 1,82,400.

Entry pay is Rs 57,700 a month as basic. Dearness allowance applies at the rate for the state, house rent allowance depends on the classification of the posting city, and transport allowance applies. Gross monthly pay at entry works out substantially above the basic figure, and the position carries the leave, medical and pension entitlements of a Madhya Pradesh government post.

Compared with the constable and clerical recruitments that dominate state hiring, this is a materially different pay bracket: entry basic here is roughly two and a half times that of a state police constable, which reflects the postgraduate and NET or PhD requirement.

## Career progression

Assistant Professor is the entry rung of the academic ladder, and progression runs through the Career Advancement Scheme rather than through a promotion exam.

| Position | Academic level |
|---|---|
| Assistant Professor (entry) | Level 10 |
| Assistant Professor (senior scale) | Level 11 |
| Assistant Professor (selection grade) | Level 12 |
| Associate Professor | Level 13A |
| Professor | Level 14 |

Movement up this ladder depends on years of service, academic performance including publications and research, refresher and orientation courses, and the screening or selection committee process laid down in the UGC regulations. Unlike a departmental promotion in an administrative service, progression here is substantially in your own hands: publication record and qualifications drive it.

## After the written exam: interview and verification

Clearing the written exam does not complete the process. Shortlisted candidates go to an interview, and then to document verification.

The interview for an academic post is not a general personality test in the way a police or administrative interview is. Expect questions on your subject, your postgraduate and doctoral work, your publications if you have any, your teaching approach, and your reasons for wanting a college post in Madhya Pradesh. Candidates who submitted a research background should be ready to defend it in detail, since a panel of subject experts will read what you claimed.

Document verification is where conditional eligibility gets tested properly. The two things that fail candidates here are a Master's percentage that falls below the 55 per cent bar once the university's own conversion formula is applied rather than the candidate's estimate, and a PhD claimed for NET exemption that does not meet the UGC regulation conditions. Both are worth checking against your actual certificates now rather than assuming.

## How this compares with other academic routes

Candidates with a NET or a PhD usually have several options open at once, and they are not equivalent.

| Route | Recruiting body | Pay entry | Selection |
|---|---|---|---|
| MPPSC Assistant Professor | Madhya Pradesh Public Service Commission | Academic Level 10 | Written exam, interview, document verification |
| Central university Assistant Professor | Individual university | Academic Level 10 | Application screening and interview, usually no written exam |
| Other state PSC Assistant Professor | State commissions | Academic Level 10 | Varies, many use written plus interview |
| Guest or contract faculty | College or university directly | Fixed monthly rate, much lower | Interview, often local |

The pay is the same across the permanent routes, so the real difference is the selection mechanism. Central universities generally shortlist on academic record and interview, which favours candidates with strong publications. State commissions like MPPSC use a written exam, which favours candidates who prepare systematically and gives a chance to those whose research record is thinner. ## CGPSC State Service Exam at a glance

CGPSC State Service Exam 2026 is the Chhattisgarh Public Service Commission's flagship recruitment cycle for 246 Group A and Group B gazetted posts across the Chhattisgarh state civil, police, revenue, cooperative, and welfare services. The exam covers Deputy Collector (Chhattisgarh State Civil Service), Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP), Block Development Officer (BDO), District Registrar, District Welfare Officer, and various allied service cadres in a state formed in 2000 with 33 districts and one of India's largest tribal populations.

The commission notified the 2026 cycle in March 2026 with the online application window running April 20, 2026 to May 20, 2026 on psc.cg.gov.in. The Preliminary Examination was scheduled for August 30, 2026, Mains in December 2026, and Interview in March 2027.

Around 1.8 lakh candidates typically appear for CGPSC State Service Exam Prelims, giving a 1 in 730 selection ratio for the 246 vacancies in this cycle. That places CGPSC in the moderate-difficulty band among state civil services exams. Deputy Collector and DSP are the two most-sought posts because they carry field-level administrative and policing authority across Chhattisgarh's diverse geography ranging from the Bastar tribal belt to the coal-mining Korba region and the industrial Raipur-Bhilai corridor.

## Posts recruited under CGPSC State Service Exam

The 246 vacancies span 7 post categories in the Group A and Group B cadres of Chhattisgarh state administration.

| Post | Group / Level | Typical initial posting |
|---|---|---|
| Deputy Collector (Chhattisgarh Civil Service) | Group A, Level 10 | Sub-Divisional Office or Tehsil headquarters |
| Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) | Group A, Level 10 | Sub-divisional police headquarters |
| Block Development Officer (BDO) | Group A, Level 10 | Block headquarters, Panchayati Raj administration |
| District Registrar | Group A, Level 10 | District registration office |
| Assistant Director (various departments) | Group A or B | State department headquarters |
| District Welfare Officer | Group B, Level 8 | District welfare cell |
| Other Group A and Group B posts | Varies | State department postings |

Deputy Collector and DSP carry the highest applicant pressure because they are field cadres with the widest career progression scope and the highest visibility in Chhattisgarh's district administration. Postings in Bastar, Sukma, Bijapur, Dantewada, and Kondagaon (the Left-Wing Extremism affected districts) carry hard-area allowances and are seen as career-defining assignments. BDO postings in the Panchayati Raj cadre are important for candidates focused on rural development in tribal sub-plan areas.

## Who qualifies for CGPSC State Service Exam

CGPSC State Service Exam has five eligibility conditions that must be satisfied on January 1, 2026.

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Nationality | Indian citizen |
| Age | 21 to 40 years for General category on January 1, 2026 |
| Education | Bachelor's degree from a UGC-recognised university, any stream |
| Language | Hindi in Devanagari script knowledge required (tested through Mains language paper) |
| Domicile | Chhattisgarh domicile required for reserved category benefits and specific tribal-quota posts |

Age relaxations follow Chhattisgarh state government norms. Chhattisgarh state government employees get 5 years extra (up to 45). Scheduled Caste, Scheduled Tribe, and Other Backward Classes candidates with Chhattisgarh domicile get 5 years extra (up to 45). Women candidates get 10 years extra over the applicable category limit (up to 50 for General women with CG domicile). Persons with Benchmark Disability (PwBD) get 5 years extra over the applicable limit. Ex-servicemen relaxations follow standard central government norms.

Chhattisgarh domicile is a hard requirement for the Scheduled Tribe reservation quota under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution and for tribal-cadre posts. Domicile is proved through the Chhattisgarh State Domicile Certificate, which requires 5 years of continuous residence in Chhattisgarh or a birth certificate showing Chhattisgarh (or undivided Madhya Pradesh, pre-2000, in specific circumstances) as the place of birth. Non-domicile applicants from other states can apply for General category posts but cannot claim tribal quota reservations.

Hindi language proficiency is tested through the Mains language paper. Candidates without Hindi-medium schooling should invest in structured Hindi essay and grammar practice before Mains. The Chhattisgarhi dialect is not tested as a separate paper, though cultural familiarity with regional dialects (Chhattisgarhi, Gondi, Halbi) is expected in the Chhattisgarh-specific General Studies content.

## Application fee and how to apply on psc.cg.gov.in

The commission charges Rs. 400 for General category and non-Chhattisgarh candidates. There is no fee for Chhattisgarh SC, ST, OBC, and PwBD candidates. Fee is paid online only through Net Banking, UPI, or credit and debit card.

1. Open psc.cg.gov.in on Chrome, Firefox, or Edge. Older browsers may fail at OTP screens.
2. Click Apply Online next to the State Service Exam 2026 notification.
3. Register with your name, date of birth, mobile number, email, and Aadhaar number exactly as they appear on your 10th class certificate.
4. Verify mobile OTP and email OTP. Both are needed.
5. Complete the personal details page including caste category, Chhattisgarh domicile status, PwBD certification if applicable, and mother tongue.
6. Fill educational qualifications with your graduation degree, university name, roll number, year of passing, and class or percentage.
7. Enter post preferences in order. You can pick up to 7 post categories. Give your most-preferred first.
8. Upload photograph (JPEG, 20 to 50 KB, taken within the last 3 months) and signature (JPEG, 10 to 20 KB, on white background).
9. Pay the application fee online. Retain the payment reference number.
10. Submit and download the Confirmation Page. Print two copies for your records.

Common errors and how to fix them. If the mobile OTP does not arrive, telecom spam filters may be blocking CGPSC SMS. Wait 5 minutes and retry, or use a different mobile number. If your photograph gets rejected for size, use online image compressors to reach the 20 to 50 KB band. If your domicile status shows a mismatch, upload the Chhattisgarh State Domicile Certificate at document verification. Post preference order is locked at submission and cannot be changed later.

## Selection process: three stages

CGPSC uses a three-stage selection process with the Preliminary Examination as a screening filter, the Main Examination as the merit-determining written test, and the Interview for evaluation of shortlisted candidates.

Stage 1 is the Preliminary Examination, which was scheduled for August 30, 2026. This is a two-paper objective test on General Studies and General Studies Aptitude Test.

| Paper | Marks | Duration | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| General Studies Paper I | 200 | 2 hours | Multiple choice, negative marking of 1 by 3 mark per wrong answer |
| General Studies Aptitude Test (Paper II) | 200 | 2 hours | Multiple choice, qualifying only at 33 percent |

Prelims Paper I is the merit-screening paper. Paper II is qualifying at 33 percent (66 out of 200). Both papers must be attempted or the candidature is void. Prelims marks do not count toward the final merit list. Around 15 times the number of Mains slots are shortlisted from Prelims.

Stage 2 is the Main Examination, a seven-paper descriptive test covering General Studies and Optional Subjects.

| Paper | Topic | Marks | Included in merit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Paper I | Language paper (Hindi and English) | 200 | Merit |
| Paper II | Essay writing | 200 | Merit |
| Paper III | History, Constitution, Public Administration, Chhattisgarh Culture | 200 | Merit |
| Paper IV | Science, Technology, Environment | 200 | Merit |
| Paper V | Economy of India and Chhattisgarh, Geography | 200 | Merit |
| Paper VI | Philosophy of India, Sociology, Governance | 200 | Merit |
| Paper VII | Optional Subject (single paper) | 200 | Merit |
| Total merit marks | | 1,400 | |

Optional Subjects are available in 22 subjects including Hindi Literature, English Literature, Sanskrit, Urdu, History, Political Science and International Relations, Public Administration, Sociology, Economics, Anthropology, Psychology, Geography, Commerce and Accountancy, Law, Botany, Zoology, Chemistry, Mathematics, Physics, Statistics, Agriculture, and Chhattisgarhi Literature.

Stage 3 is the Interview or Personality Test held at the CGPSC office in Raipur. Marks weightage is 150 for all Group A posts. Total maximum marks for merit calculation is 1,400 (Mains) + 150 (Interview) = 1,550.

## Detailed syllabus and recommended books

CGPSC State Service Exam syllabus overlaps significantly with UPSC Civil Services on core General Studies, but Chhattisgarh-specific tribal culture, mineral economy, Fifth Schedule Bastar administration, and Chhattisgarhi cultural heritage are the differentiators.

Prelims General Studies Paper I covers eight areas. Indian Economy (five-year plans, Chhattisgarh economy including coal at Korba, iron ore at Bailadila, and NMDC mining royalty). Science and Technology (general awareness, mining and metallurgy focus, BHEL Bhilai steel plant). General Awareness (schemes, sports, awards). Hira Lal Shukla "History of Chhattisgarh" for state-specific historical coverage. Verrier Elwin's works on Bastar for tribal ethnography. Laxmikanth "Indian Polity" for constitutional topics, with special attention to Fifth Schedule and PESA. NCERT Class 11 and 12 for economics and geography basics. Yojana magazine and Chhattisgarh PIB releases for current affairs.

Mains merit papers reward structured answers with introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion. Practise writing at least 5 answers per week during the last 3 months before Mains. Paper II Essay commonly features Chhattisgarh-specific topics (mining royalty and displacement, Bastar development, tribal welfare, Naxal insurgency and Salwa Judum legacy, Mahtari Vandana Yojana impact, forest rights) alongside national themes.

Native Chhattisgarhi speakers can consider Chhattisgarhi Literature (available as a distinct optional). ## Salary breakdown and career progression

CGPSC-recruited officers start at Pay Level 8 to Level 10 depending on the post, under the 7th Central Pay Commission structure adopted by Chhattisgarh.

| Post | Basic pay (7th CPC) | Gross monthly | In-hand monthly |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deputy Collector, DSP, BDO, District Registrar (Level 10) | Rs. 56,100 | Rs. 82,000 to Rs. 92,000 | Rs. 68,000 to Rs. 76,000 |
| Assistant Director, Group A allied (Level 10) | Rs. 56,100 | Rs. 80,000 to Rs. 90,000 | Rs. 66,000 to Rs. 74,000 |
| District Welfare Officer (Level 8) | Rs. 47,600 | Rs. 70,000 to Rs. 80,000 | Rs. 60,000 to Rs. 66,000 |

Gross pay includes Dearness Allowance (currently 50 percent of basic under central and Chhattisgarh state norms), House Rent Allowance (24 percent for Raipur and Bhilai, 16 percent for other municipal areas, 8 percent elsewhere), Transport Allowance (Rs. 7,200 to Rs. 15,000 per month based on city class), and Chhattisgarh-specific allowances including tribal area allowance for Fifth Schedule postings (Bastar, Sukma, Bijapur, Dantewada, Kondagaon).

Reaching Chief Secretary (Level 17) requires IAS deputation through a Union Public Service Commission promotion process, typically after 15 to 20 years of state service.

DSP progression moves through Sub-Divisional Police Officer, Additional Superintendent of Police, Superintendent of Police in a district, Deputy Inspector General at range level, and Inspector General at zonal level over 20 to 25 years. Reaching Director General of Police requires Indian Police Service deputation.

BDO promotions go through Additional District Development Commissioner, Additional District Magistrate (Development), and Divisional Commissioner over 20 to 25 years. Month 3-4: Deep-dive into Indian and Chhattisgarh Geography (Mahanadi basin, Bastar plateau, mineral belt including coal at Korba and iron ore at Bailadila) and Economy (Indian and Chhattisgarh, including NMDC mining royalty, BHEL Bhilai, Vishnu Deo Sai era schemes, Mahtari Vandana Yojana). Begin Optional Subject preparation in parallel; aim for 2 to 3 hours per day. Write 3 answers per week on GS topics.

Month 5-6: Focus on Language Paper preparation (Hindi and English), especially if you did not study Hindi beyond Matriculation. Read a standard Hindi grammar text daily and write one essay per week. Continue Optional Subject deep-dive.

Month 7: Prelims focused mode. Daily current affairs revision, mock tests every 3 days, detailed Chhattisgarh GK sweep (chief ministers, Vishnu Deo Sai era schemes, Mahtari Vandana rollout status, budget highlights, Naxal insurgency updates, Bastar development). Prelims on August 30, 2026 sits at the end of this window.

Under-preparing Chhattisgarh-specific General Knowledge. Standard UPSC preparation material has minimal Chhattisgarh coverage. CGPSC Prelims and Mains together carry 30 to 40 questions on Chhattisgarh directly (chief ministers, Vishnu Deo Sai era schemes, Mahtari Vandana, Bastar, Naxal insurgency, mining royalty). Missing this is the single biggest score gap.

Wrong Optional Subject choice. Picking a subject you never studied at graduation and cannot cover in 6 months is a self-inflicted wound. Native Chhattisgarhi speakers should seriously consider Chhattisgarhi Literature. Anthropology has particularly strong Bastar tribal coverage and is a popular Optional for candidates targeting tribal-cadre posts.

Ignoring the Language Paper I. It carries 200 merit marks (roughly 14 percent of merit ceiling). Poor Hindi or English writing costs 40 to 50 marks that could otherwise be secured with 3 months of structured essay practice.

Skipping the Prelims Paper II (Aptitude Test) preparation. Paper II is qualifying only, but failing to score 33 percent (66 out of 200) disqualifies from Prelims regardless of Paper I score.

Ignoring Chhattisgarh current affairs. National current affairs are covered by every candidate. Chhattisgarh-specific current affairs (state budget, Vishnu Deo Sai era schemes, court judgments on state issues including the Mahtari Vandana eKYC drive coverage, Bastar development, mining royalty updates) differentiate serious candidates. | Mains merit marks | 1,400 | 1,750 |
| Interview marks | 150 | 275 |
| Total merit ceiling | 1,550 | 2,025 |

Indian citizens aged 21 to 40 (General category on January 1, 2026) with a Bachelor's degree from a UGC-recognised university. 9. Pay the application fee online. Retain the payment reference number.
10. Submit and download the Confirmation Page. Print two copies for your records.

Daily current affairs revision, mock tests every 3 days, detailed Chhattisgarh GK sweep (chief ministers, Vishnu Deo Sai era schemes, Mahtari Vandana rollout status, budget highlights, Naxal insurgency updates, Bastar development). Prelims on August 30, 2026 sits at the end of this window.

Month 8-11 (post-Prelims): Full Mains preparation mode. Answer writing practice for all six GS papers, Essay paper, and the Optional Subject paper. Hindi and English Compulsory daily 1-hour practice. Interview preparation from Month 10 onwards for candidates confident of Mains qualification.

Candidates with prior UPSC preparation can compress the plan to 8 months by focusing on Chhattisgarh-specific content, Fifth Schedule and Bastar administration, and the Optional Subject, since UPSC prep covers the core GS syllabus adequately.

## Common mistakes candidates make

Seven mistakes account for most CGPSC State Service Exam rejections across cycles.

Under-preparing Chhattisgarh-specific General Knowledge. Standard UPSC preparation material has minimal Chhattisgarh coverage. CGPSC Prelims and Mains together carry 30 to 40 questions on Chhattisgarh directly (chief ministers, Vishnu Deo Sai era schemes, Mahtari Vandana, Bastar, Naxal insurgency, mining royalty). Missing this is the single biggest score gap.

Wrong Optional Subject choice. Picking a subject you never studied at graduation and cannot cover in 6 months is a self-inflicted wound. Native Chhattisgarhi speakers should seriously consider Chhattisgarhi Literature. Anthropology has particularly strong Bastar tribal coverage and is a popular Optional for candidates targeting tribal-cadre posts.

Ignoring the Language Paper I. It carries 200 merit marks (roughly 14 percent of merit ceiling). Poor Hindi or English writing costs 40 to 50 marks that could otherwise be secured with 3 months of structured essay practice.

Skipping the Prelims Paper II (Aptitude Test) preparation. Paper II is qualifying only, but failing to score 33 percent (66 out of 200) disqualifies from Prelims regardless of Paper I score.

Missing the Chhattisgarh domicile certificate at document verification. Candidates who claim ST reservation for tribal quota posts must present the Chhattisgarh State Domicile Certificate at document verification. Missing this document triggers a downgrade to General category or full disqualification from tribal-quota posts.

Post preference order errors. The commission allocates posts based on merit rank and preference order at application. Putting District Welfare Officer as first preference when the real target is Deputy Collector is a common mistake that gets locked at application and cannot be changed later.

Ignoring Chhattisgarh current affairs. National current affairs are covered by every candidate. Chhattisgarh-specific current affairs (state budget, Vishnu Deo Sai era schemes, court judgments on state issues including the Mahtari Vandana eKYC drive coverage, Bastar development, mining royalty updates) differentiate serious candidates. Read Deshbandhu or Nai Duniya daily.

## CGPSC State Service vs UPSC Civil Services

CGPSC State Service and UPSC CSE overlap significantly on syllabus but diverge on scale, competition, and career trajectory. This comparison helps candidates decide whether to target CGPSC as primary or as backup to UPSC.

| Feature | CGPSC State Service 2026 | UPSC Civil Services 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Vacancies | 246 | 1,056 |
| Selection ratio | 1 in 730 | 1 in 800 |
| Age (General) | 21 to 40 | 21 to 32 |
| Attempts limit | No cap, only age ceiling | 6 for General, 9 for OBC, unlimited for SC/ST |
| Prelims marks | 400 (Paper I 200 merit + Paper II 200 qualifying) | 400 |
| Mains merit marks | 1,400 | 1,750 |
| Interview marks | 150 | 275 |
| Total merit ceiling | 1,550 | 2,025 |
| Salary entry (Level 10) | Rs. 56,100 basic | Rs. 56,100 basic |
| Career ceiling | Principal Secretary, IAS deputation rare | Cabinet Secretary direct |
| Home state posting | Guaranteed (Chhattisgarh cadre) | Depends on cadre allocation |
| Prep time typical | 8 to 14 months | 12 to 24 months |
| Syllabus overlap | 75 percent with UPSC CSE | Baseline |
| Language paper | Language Paper I 200 (merit) | Indian language + English 300 each (qualifying) |
| Unique optional | Chhattisgarhi Literature available | None |

CGPSC State Service is the right primary target for candidates with Chhattisgarh domicile ties who prioritise home state posting and want a shorter preparation timeline than UPSC. UPSC is the right primary target for candidates aiming at national-level cadres. Many candidates prepare for both in parallel because the syllabus overlap is around 75 percent. The Chhattisgarhi Literature optional is a rare offering unavailable in most other state PSC exams and provides a native-fluency scoring advantage.

## Frequently asked questions

**Who is eligible for CGPSC State Service Exam 2026?**
Indian citizens aged 21 to 40 (General category on January 1, 2026) with a Bachelor's degree from a UGC-recognised university. Chhattisgarh state government employees get 5 years extra, SC / ST / OBC candidates with CG domicile get 5 years extra (up to 45), women get 10 years extra (up to 50 for General women with CG domicile), and PwBD get 5 years extra.

**How many vacancies are in CGPSC State Service Exam 2026?**
246 vacancies across 7 post categories including Deputy Collector (Chhattisgarh Civil Service), Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP), Block Development Officer (BDO), District Registrar, Assistant Director, District Welfare Officer, and other Group A and B allied posts.

**What is the last date to apply for CGPSC State Service Exam 2026?**
May 20, 2026. Online applications open April 20, 2026 on psc.cg.gov.in. The Preliminary Examination was scheduled for August 30, 2026.

**Is Chhattisgarh domicile required for CGPSC State Service Exam?**
Not for base eligibility. Any Indian citizen aged 21 to 40 with a Bachelor's degree can apply. Chhattisgarh State Domicile Certificate is required for Scheduled Tribe reservation quota and for a subset of tribal-cadre posts under the Fifth Schedule. Chhattisgarh SC, ST, OBC, and women candidates need domicile for extended age relaxations.

**How much is the application fee?**
Rs. 400 for General category and non-Chhattisgarh candidates. Free for Chhattisgarh SC, ST, OBC, and PwBD candidates. Payment is online only through Net Banking, UPI, or credit and debit card.

**What is the exam pattern for CGPSC State Service Exam?**
Three stages. Prelims is two 200-mark papers (Paper I merit-screening, Paper II Aptitude Test qualifying at 33 percent). Mains is seven papers of 200 marks each including Language Paper I, Essay Paper II, four GS papers (III to VI), and one Optional Subject paper (VII), totalling 1,400 merit marks. Interview carries 150 marks. Total merit ceiling is 1,550.

**Can I choose Chhattisgarhi Literature as my Mains optional?**
Yes. Paper VII Optional Subject includes Chhattisgarhi Literature along with 21 other subjects. Native Chhattisgarhi speakers should consider this option because native fluency reduces preparation time and offers strong scoring potential.

**What is the salary of a CGPSC Deputy Collector?**
Pay Level 10, basic pay Rs. 56,100 under the 7th Central Pay Commission structure. Gross monthly Rs. 82,000 to Rs. 92,000 including DA at 50 percent, HRA at 24 percent for Raipur and Bhilai, tribal area allowance for Fifth Schedule postings in Bastar, and other allowances. In-hand around Rs. 68,000 to Rs. 76,000 after standard deductions.

**Can I become an IAS officer through CGPSC?**
Not directly. CGPSC recruits into Chhattisgarh state services. IAS deputation is available to a small fraction of Chhattisgarh Civil Service officers who clear a Union Public Service Commission promotion process later in their career, typically after 15 to 20 years of state service.

**Should I prepare for CGPSC alongside UPSC Civil Services?**
Yes if you have Chhattisgarh domicile ties. The syllabus overlap is around 75 percent. Add Chhattisgarh-specific General Knowledge (2 hours per day for 2 months), study Fifth Schedule and Bastar administration, and choose an Optional Subject you graduated in or take Chhattisgarhi Literature if you speak it natively. Many candidates clear CGPSC as a fallback while continuing UPSC attempts.

## SSC MTS 2026 at a glance

The Staff Selection Commission released the SSC MTS and Havaldar 2026 notification on 30 June 2026 for 7,948 posts, and the online application window closed on 31 July 2026. If you hold a Class 10 pass certificate and want a permanent central government job with no interview stage, this is one of the few large recruitments open right now.

The recruitment fills two post groups: Multi-Tasking (Non-Technical) Staff across central government departments, and Havaldar in the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) and the Central Bureau of Narcotics (CBN). Of the 7,948 vacancies, roughly 6,810 are MTS posts and 1,138 are Havaldar posts, per the SSC MTS 2026 notification.

One number sets the tone for how competitive this is. In the 2024 cycle SSC received well over 50 lakh applications for a similar vacancy pool, which works out to more than 600 candidates chasing each seat. The exam is Class 10 standard, but the cutoff is high precisely because the paper is easy and the field is enormous.

For candidates who have finished Class 10 and want a stable central government job without a graduation requirement or an interview, SSC MTS is one of the shortest routes in. The trade-off is that the entry pay is modest and the competition is heavy, so the difference between a seat and a near-miss usually comes down to a handful of marks in the second session. The rest of this guide covers every stage in detail, from the vacancy split and eligibility to the exam pattern, the worked in-hand salary, the cutoff trend, and how the job compares with SSC GD and CHSL.

## Important dates for SSC MTS 2026

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Notification released | 30 June 2026 |
| Online application begins | 30 June 2026 |
| Last date to apply | 31 July 2026 |
| Last date for fee payment | 31 July 2026 (11:00 PM) |
| Application correction window | Early August 2026 (per SSC notice) |
| Computer Based Test (Session I and II) | September to November 2026, per the SSC Exam Calendar |
| Age reckoned as on | 1 August 2026 |

Dates for the correction window and the exact CBT day are announced on ssc.gov.in through separate notices, so keep checking the login dashboard after you submit the form.

## Vacancy details

The 7,948 vacancies split across two age bands and the Havaldar cadre. The two MTS age groups exist because certain user departments set an 18 to 25 band while others use 18 to 27.

| Post | Age group | Approx vacancies |
|---|---|---|
| Multi-Tasking Staff (MTS) | 18 to 25 years | 6,078 |
| Multi-Tasking Staff (MTS) | 18 to 27 years | 732 |
| Havaldar (CBIC and CBN) | 18 to 27 years | 1,138 |
| Total | | 7,948 |

For context on the trend, SSC notified 7,948 posts in the 2025 cycle, 11,518 in 2024, and 11,788 in 2023, per successive SSC notifications. The count moves with departmental demand each year, so treat the 2026 figure as the confirmed number and ignore any inflated projections you see on coaching pages.

## Eligibility for SSC MTS 2026

Age limit reads off the age group you apply for. Most MTS posts need 18 to 25 years as on 1 August 2026. Havaldar and some MTS posts allow 18 to 27 years. Category relaxation follows standard government norms.

| Category | Age relaxation |
|---|---|
| OBC (non-creamy layer) | 3 years |
| SC and ST | 5 years |
| PwBD (unreserved) | 10 years |
| PwBD (OBC) | 13 years |
| PwBD (SC and ST) | 15 years |
| Ex-servicemen | As per service rules |

On qualification, the bar is a Class 10 (Matriculation) pass from a recognised board. A higher degree does not help or hurt your eligibility, and there is no minimum percentage. Nationality rules follow the usual clauses for Indian citizens plus the standard provisions for subjects of Nepal and Bhutan and Tibetan refugees who settled in India before 1962.

## Application fee

The fee is modest and waived for several categories, including all women candidates.

| Category | Fee |
|---|---|
| General, OBC, EWS | Rs 100 |
| SC, ST, PwBD, ex-servicemen | Nil |
| All women candidates | Nil |

Pay online through BHIM UPI, net banking, or a debit or credit card. There is no offline challan option in the current cycle.

## Selection process

The MTS and Havaldar selection runs on a Computer Based Test with two sessions on the same day. There is no interview and no descriptive paper.

The stages are:

1. Computer Based Test, Session I and Session II, both compulsory for every candidate.
2. Physical Efficiency Test and Physical Standard Test (PET and PST), for Havaldar applicants only. This stage is qualifying.
3. Document verification, for candidates who clear the earlier stages.

Session I carries no negative marking, which makes it a section where you attempt everything. Session II carries a penalty of 1 mark for each wrong answer, so guesswork there costs you. That single design choice decides a lot of strategy, and most candidates who miss the cutoff do so by over-attempting Session II.

## Exam pattern

Both sessions run back to back. The full paper is 90 questions for 270 marks in 90 minutes, offered in English, Hindi, and 13 regional languages.

| Session | Subject | Questions | Marks | Duration | Negative marking |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | Numerical and mathematical ability | 20 | 60 | 45 min | None |
| I | Reasoning ability and problem solving | 20 | 60 | 45 min | None |
| II | General awareness | 25 | 75 | 45 min | 1 mark per wrong answer |
| II | English language and comprehension | 25 | 75 | 45 min | 1 mark per wrong answer |
| Total | | 90 | 270 | 90 min | Session II only |

Candidates who use a scribe get 60 minutes per session instead of 45. Session I acts as a screening qualifier and Session II decides the merit position within your category and age group.

## Syllabus for SSC MTS 2026

The paper stays at Class 10 standard across all four subjects. Depth matters less than speed and accuracy.

Numerical and mathematical ability covers integers, LCM and HCF, decimals and fractions, BODMAS, percentage, ratio and proportion, profit and loss, simple interest, averages, time and work, time speed and distance, and basic mensuration.

Reasoning ability and problem solving covers analogies, series completion, coding and decoding, classification, non-verbal patterns, direction sense, and blood relations.

General awareness covers current affairs (usually 7 to 8 questions), biology, history, polity, geography, economics, static general knowledge, sports, and awards. This is the section that separates candidates, since it rewards steady daily reading.

English language and comprehension covers reading comprehension, grammar, vocabulary, spotting errors, sentence structure, and synonyms and antonyms.

## SSC MTS 2026 salary and in-hand pay

MTS and Havaldar posts sit at Pay Level 1 of the 7th Pay Commission, with a basic pay of Rs 18,000 and a scale of Rs 18,000 to Rs 56,900. The number that matters to you is the in-hand figure after dearness allowance, house rent allowance, and transport allowance, minus deductions.

Dearness allowance rose to 60 percent of basic pay effective 1 January 2026, per the Finance Ministry order. Many coaching pages still show a stale 17 to 50 percent DA, which understates the salary. Here is the worked in-hand pay at the current 60 percent DA, split by city class (X, Y, Z), for a Level 1 recruit.

| Component | X city (metro) | Y city | Z city |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic pay | Rs 18,000 | Rs 18,000 | Rs 18,000 |
| Dearness allowance (60%) | Rs 10,800 | Rs 10,800 | Rs 10,800 |
| House rent allowance (30 / 20 / 10%) | Rs 5,400 | Rs 3,600 | Rs 1,800 |
| Transport allowance (with DA) | Rs 2,160 | Rs 2,160 | Rs 1,440 |
| Gross | Rs 36,360 | Rs 34,560 | Rs 32,040 |
| Deductions (NPS, CGEGIS, CGHS) | about Rs 3,200 | about Rs 3,200 | about Rs 3,100 |
| Approx in-hand | about Rs 33,200 | about Rs 31,400 | about Rs 28,900 |

So a fresh MTS recruit posted in a metro takes home roughly Rs 33,000 a month, and the figure climbs every time DA is revised. Havaldar pay sits at the same Level 1, with the added duty profile of customs and narcotics field work.

## Havaldar PET and PST standards

Havaldar applicants clear a Physical Efficiency Test and a Physical Standard Test after the CBT. This stage is qualifying, not merit-deciding, but you cannot be appointed without passing it.

| Test | Male | Female |
|---|---|---|
| PET walk | 1,600 m in 15 minutes | 1 km in 20 minutes |
| PST height | 157.5 cm | 152 cm |
| PST chest (male) | 81 cm with 5 cm expansion | Not applicable |

Height relaxations of about 5 cm for men and 2.5 cm for women apply to candidates from hill communities such as Garhwalis, Assamese, and Gorkhas, and to Scheduled Tribe candidates.

## SSC MTS cutoff trend

Cutoffs vary by category, state, and age group, and they run high because the paper is easy. As a reference point, the All India unreserved cutoff for the 18 to 25 group sat near 147.78 marks in a recent cycle, per SSC result data.

| Category | Indicative cutoff (out of 270) |
|---|---|
| Unreserved (UR) | 142 to 152 |
| OBC | 138 to 145 |
| EWS | 134 to 140 |
| SC | 128 to 138 |
| ST | 120 to 132 |

Treat these as a planning band, not a promise. Your state and age group shift the exact figure, and the 18 to 27 pool usually closes at a slightly different mark than the 18 to 25 pool.

## SSC MTS vs SSC GD vs SSC CHSL

Candidates eligible for MTS often weigh it against [SSC GD Constable](/sarkari-naukri/ssc-gd-constable-2026) and [SSC CHSL](/sarkari-naukri/ssc-chsl-2026). This comparison sets out the real differences.

| Factor | SSC MTS | SSC GD Constable | SSC CHSL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum qualification | Class 10 | Class 10 | Class 12 |
| Pay Level | Level 1 (Rs 18,000) | Level 3 (about Rs 21,700) | Level 2 or 4 (Rs 19,900 to Rs 25,500) |
| Approx in-hand | Rs 29,000 to 33,000 | Rs 30,000 to 36,000 | Rs 30,000 to 40,000 |
| Nature of work | Office and support duties | Uniformed CAPF service | Clerical and data entry |
| Physical test | Havaldar posts only | Yes, for all posts | No |
| Promotion path | MTS to LDC to UDC to Section Officer | Constable to Head Constable to ASI | LDC or DEO to UDC to divisional cadre |

MTS suits candidates who want a stable desk job close to home with no physical test. SSC GD suits those ready for uniformed field service, and CHSL fits Class 12 pass candidates who want clerical roles at a slightly higher pay level.

## Career growth and promotions

An MTS recruit does not stay at Level 1. The typical ladder runs from MTS to Lower Division Clerk after about three years of service, then Upper Division Clerk, then Divisional Clerk, and up to Section Officer over a full career, with pay increments at each step. Havaldar recruits in CBIC and CBN handle field duties tied to customs checks and narcotics control, and they follow their own promotion track within those departments.

## Choosing your post and centre preference

The application form asks you to rank your post and department preferences and pick an examination centre. Two things are worth thinking about before you fill this in. First, the two MTS age bands (18 to 25 and 18 to 27) draw from different departmental vacancy pools, so your date of birth decides which posts you compete for. Second, Havaldar carries the physical test, so opt for it only if you can clear the walk and the height and chest standards, since a good CBT score is wasted if you fail the PET or PST. Pick a centre you can reach comfortably on exam day, because SSC rarely changes it once allotted, and a long commute on the morning of a two-session paper works against you.

## How to apply for SSC MTS 2026

1. Register on the SSC OTR (One Time Registration) portal at ssc.gov.in if you have not already.
2. Log in and open the SSC MTS and Havaldar 2026 application link.
3. Fill in personal, educational, and category details, and select your post preference and examination centre.
4. Upload a recent photograph and signature in the specified format.
5. Pay the Rs 100 fee if you fall in the paying category. Women and reserved categories pay nothing.
6. Submit before 31 July 2026 and save the confirmation page for your records.

## Documents required for the application

Keep these ready before you open the form, since the portal times out if you hunt for files midway.

1. A scanned passport-size photograph taken recently, in the size and format SSC specifies.
2. A scanned signature on white paper.
3. Your Class 10 certificate for the date of birth and qualification details.
4. A category certificate (OBC, SC, ST, EWS, or PwBD) if you claim relaxation.
5. Aadhaar or another government photo ID for the One Time Registration.
6. A working email and mobile number, since all admit card and result alerts go there.

## Admit card and exam day

SSC releases the admit card region by region, roughly 7 to 10 days before your CBT date, through the regional SSC website and your login dashboard. Download it, check that your name, photograph, category, and centre are correct, and carry a printout with the same photo ID you used at registration. Reach the centre early, since biometric and frisking checks take time and latecomers are turned away. Rough sheets are provided inside, and you must hand them back before leaving.

## Answer key, normalization, and result

After the CBT, SSC publishes a provisional answer key with an objection window, where you can challenge a wrong key for a small per-question fee that is refunded if your objection is upheld. Because the exam runs across many shifts and days, SSC applies normalization: your raw score is adjusted for the relative difficulty of your shift, so two candidates with the same raw marks in different shifts can end with different normalized scores. The merit list uses these normalized Session II scores within your category and age group. Keep an eye on the SSC website for the result, the marks release, and the document verification schedule, since each is announced through a separate notice.

## Building a study plan

Treat the last eight to ten weeks as a rehearsal, not a first read. Give the first half of that window to finishing every topic once and building speed on maths and reasoning, where Session I has no negative marking and rewards a full attempt. Give the second half to full-length mock tests taken at the same time of day as your slot, followed by a careful review of every wrong answer. For general awareness, a single daily current affairs source plus a static general knowledge booklet covers most of what the paper asks. English improves fastest through daily reading and a fixed set of grammar rules rather than memorising word lists. The candidates who convert this exam are rarely the ones who studied the most. They are the ones who made the fewest careless errors in Session II.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the last date to apply for SSC MTS 2026?**
The last date to apply for SSC MTS 2026 is 31 July 2026, with fee payment also closing on the same day at 11:00 PM. The notification was released on 30 June 2026.

**How many vacancies are there in SSC MTS 2026?**
SSC MTS 2026 has 7,948 vacancies, split into roughly 6,810 Multi-Tasking Staff posts and 1,138 Havaldar posts in CBIC and CBN, per the SSC MTS 2026 notification.

**Is there negative marking in SSC MTS 2026?**
Yes, but only in Session II. General awareness and English carry a penalty of 1 mark per wrong answer, while Session I (maths and reasoning) has no negative marking, so you can attempt every question there.

**What is the in-hand salary of SSC MTS in 2026?**
A Level 1 MTS recruit takes home about Rs 33,000 a month in a metro (X city) at the 60 percent dearness allowance effective 1 January 2026, and about Rs 29,000 in a Z-class city, after standard deductions.

**What is the qualification needed for SSC MTS?**
A Class 10 (Matriculation) pass from a recognised board is the only qualification needed for SSC MTS. There is no minimum percentage and no upper degree requirement.

**Who has to appear for the PET and PST in SSC MTS?**
Only Havaldar applicants appear for the Physical Efficiency Test and Physical Standard Test. Multi-Tasking Staff posts have no physical test, and the Havaldar PET and PST are qualifying rather than merit-deciding.

**How is the SSC MTS age limit calculated?**
Age is reckoned as on 1 August 2026. Most MTS posts need 18 to 25 years, while Havaldar and some MTS posts allow 18 to 27 years, with category relaxations of 3 years for OBC, 5 years for SC and ST, and up to 15 years for PwBD.

**What is the difference between MTS and Havaldar?**
MTS involves office and support duties across central government departments at Pay Level 1, while Havaldar is a field role in customs (CBIC) and narcotics control (CBN) at the same pay level, with an added physical test at selection.

| General, OBC, EWS | Rs 100 |
| SC, ST, PwBD, ex-servicemen | Nil |
| All women candidates | Nil |

Pay online through BHIM UPI, net banking, or a debit or credit card. There is no offline challan option in the current cycle.

## Selection process

The MTS and Havaldar selection runs on a Computer Based Test with two sessions on the same day. There is no interview and no descriptive paper.

The stages are:

1. Computer Based Test, Session I and Session II, both compulsory for every candidate.
2. Physical Efficiency Test and Physical Standard Test (PET and PST), for Havaldar applicants only. This stage is qualifying.
3. Document verification, for candidates who clear the earlier stages.

Session I carries no negative marking, which makes it a section where you attempt everything. Session II carries a penalty of 1 mark for each wrong answer, so guesswork there costs you. That single design choice decides a lot of strategy, and most candidates who miss the cutoff do so by over-attempting Session II.

## Exam pattern

Both sessions run back to back. The full paper is 90 questions for 270 marks in 90 minutes, offered in English, Hindi, and 13 regional languages.

| Session | Subject | Questions | Marks | Duration | Negative marking |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| I | Numerical and mathematical ability | 20 | 60 | 45 min | None |
| I | Reasoning ability and problem solving | 20 | 60 | 45 min | None |
| II | General awareness | 25 | 75 | 45 min | 1 mark per wrong answer |
| II | English language and comprehension | 25 | 75 | 45 min | 1 mark per wrong answer |
| Total | | 90 | 270 | 90 min | Session II only |

Candidates who use a scribe get 60 minutes per session instead of 45. Session I acts as a screening qualifier and Session II decides the merit position within your category and age group.

## Syllabus for SSC MTS 2026

The paper stays at Class 10 standard across all four subjects. Depth matters less than speed and accuracy.

Numerical and mathematical ability covers integers, LCM and HCF, decimals and fractions, BODMAS, percentage, ratio and proportion, profit and loss, simple interest, averages, time and work, time speed and distance, and basic mensuration.

Reasoning ability and problem solving covers analogies, series completion, coding and decoding, classification, non-verbal patterns, direction sense, and blood relations.

General awareness covers current affairs (usually 7 to 8 questions), biology, history, polity, geography, economics, static general knowledge, sports, and awards. This is the section that separates candidates, since it rewards steady daily reading.

English language and comprehension covers reading comprehension, grammar, vocabulary, spotting errors, sentence structure, and synonyms and antonyms.

## SSC MTS 2026 salary and in-hand pay

MTS and Havaldar posts sit at Pay Level 1 of the 7th Pay Commission, with a basic pay of Rs 18,000 and a scale of Rs 18,000 to Rs 56,900. The number that matters to you is the in-hand figure after dearness allowance, house rent allowance, and transport allowance, minus deductions.

Dearness allowance rose to 60 percent of basic pay effective 1 January 2026, per the Finance Ministry order. Many coaching pages still show a stale 17 to 50 percent DA, which understates the salary. Here is the worked in-hand pay at the current 60 percent DA, split by city class (X, Y, Z), for a Level 1 recruit.

| Component | X city (metro) | Y city | Z city |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic pay | Rs 18,000 | Rs 18,000 | Rs 18,000 |
| Dearness allowance (60%) | Rs 10,800 | Rs 10,800 | Rs 10,800 |
| House rent allowance (30 / 20 / 10%) | Rs 5,400 | Rs 3,600 | Rs 1,800 |
| Transport allowance (with DA) | Rs 2,160 | Rs 2,160 | Rs 1,440 |
| Gross | Rs 36,360 | Rs 34,560 | Rs 32,040 |
| Deductions (NPS, CGEGIS, CGHS) | about Rs 3,200 | about Rs 3,200 | about Rs 3,100 |
| Approx in-hand | about Rs 33,200 | about Rs 31,400 | about Rs 28,900 |

So a fresh MTS recruit posted in a metro takes home roughly Rs 33,000 a month, and the figure climbs every time DA is revised. Havaldar pay sits at the same Level 1, with the added duty profile of customs and narcotics field work.

## Havaldar PET and PST standards

Havaldar applicants clear a Physical Efficiency Test and a Physical Standard Test after the CBT. This stage is qualifying, not merit-deciding, but you cannot be appointed without passing it.

| Test | Male | Female |
|---|---|---|
| PET walk | 1,600 m in 15 minutes | 1 km in 20 minutes |
| PST height | 157.5 cm | 152 cm |
| PST chest (male) | 81 cm with 5 cm expansion | Not applicable |

Height relaxations of about 5 cm for men and 2.5 cm for women apply to candidates from hill communities such as Garhwalis, Assamese, and Gorkhas, and to Scheduled Tribe candidates.

## SSC MTS cutoff trend

Cutoffs vary by category, state, and age group, and they run high because the paper is easy. As a reference point, the All India unreserved cutoff for the 18 to 25 group sat near 147.78 marks in a recent cycle, per SSC result data.

| Category | Indicative cutoff (out of 270) |
|---|---|
| Unreserved (UR) | 142 to 152 |
| OBC | 138 to 145 |
| EWS | 134 to 140 |
| SC | 128 to 138 |
| ST | 120 to 132 |

Treat these as a planning band, not a promise. Your state and age group shift the exact figure, and the 18 to 27 pool usually closes at a slightly different mark than the 18 to 25 pool.

## SSC MTS vs SSC GD vs SSC CHSL

Candidates eligible for MTS often weigh it against [SSC GD Constable](/sarkari-naukri/ssc-gd-constable-2026) and [SSC CHSL](/sarkari-naukri/ssc-chsl-2026). This comparison sets out the real differences.

| Factor | SSC MTS | SSC GD Constable | SSC CHSL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum qualification | Class 10 | Class 10 | Class 12 |
| Pay Level | Level 1 (Rs 18,000) | Level 3 (about Rs 21,700) | Level 2 or 4 (Rs 19,900 to Rs 25,500) |
| Approx in-hand | Rs 29,000 to 33,000 | Rs 30,000 to 36,000 | Rs 30,000 to 40,000 |
| Nature of work | Office and support duties | Uniformed CAPF service | Clerical and data entry |
| Physical test | Havaldar posts only | Yes, for all posts | No |
| Promotion path | MTS to LDC to UDC to Section Officer | Constable to Head Constable to ASI | LDC or DEO to UDC to divisional cadre |

MTS suits candidates who want a stable desk job close to home with no physical test. SSC GD suits those ready for uniformed field service, and CHSL fits Class 12 pass candidates who want clerical roles at a slightly higher pay level.

## Career growth and promotions

An MTS recruit does not stay at Level 1. The typical ladder runs from MTS to Lower Division Clerk after about three years of service, then Upper Division Clerk, then Divisional Clerk, and up to Section Officer over a full career, with pay increments at each step. Havaldar recruits in CBIC and CBN handle field duties tied to customs checks and narcotics control, and they follow their own promotion track within those departments.

## Choosing your post and centre preference

The application form asks you to rank your post and department preferences and pick an examination centre. Two things are worth thinking about before you fill this in. First, the two MTS age bands (18 to 25 and 18 to 27) draw from different departmental vacancy pools, so your date of birth decides which posts you compete for. Second, Havaldar carries the physical test, so opt for it only if you can clear the walk and the height and chest standards, since a good CBT score is wasted if you fail the PET or PST. Pick a centre you can reach comfortably on exam day, because SSC rarely changes it once allotted, and a long commute on the morning of a two-session paper works against you.

## How to apply for SSC MTS 2026

1. Register on the SSC OTR (One Time Registration) portal at ssc.gov.in if you have not already.
2. Log in and open the SSC MTS and Havaldar 2026 application link.
3. Fill in personal, educational, and category details, and select your post preference and examination centre.
4. Upload a recent photograph and signature in the specified format.
5. Pay the Rs 100 fee if you fall in the paying category. Women and reserved categories pay nothing.
6. Submit before 31 July 2026 and save the confirmation page for your records.

## Documents required for the application

Keep these ready before you open the form, since the portal times out if you hunt for files midway.

1. A scanned passport-size photograph taken recently, in the size and format SSC specifies.
2. A scanned signature on white paper.
3. Your Class 10 certificate for the date of birth and qualification details.
4. A category certificate (OBC, SC, ST, EWS, or PwBD) if you claim relaxation.
5. Aadhaar or another government photo ID for the One Time Registration.
6. A working email and mobile number, since all admit card and result alerts go there.

## Admit card and exam day

SSC releases the admit card region by region, roughly 7 to 10 days before your CBT date, through the regional SSC website and your login dashboard. Download it, check that your name, photograph, category, and centre are correct, and carry a printout with the same photo ID you used at registration. Reach the centre early, since biometric and frisking checks take time and latecomers are turned away. Rough sheets are provided inside, and you must hand them back before leaving.

## Answer key, normalization, and result

After the CBT, SSC publishes a provisional answer key with an objection window, where you can challenge a wrong key for a small per-question fee that is refunded if your objection is upheld. Because the exam runs across many shifts and days, SSC applies normalization: your raw score is adjusted for the relative difficulty of your shift, so two candidates with the same raw marks in different shifts can end with different normalized scores. The merit list uses these normalized Session II scores within your category and age group. Keep an eye on the SSC website for the result, the marks release, and the document verification schedule, since each is announced through a separate notice.

## Building a study plan

Treat the last eight to ten weeks as a rehearsal, not a first read. Give the first half of that window to finishing every topic once and building speed on maths and reasoning, where Session I has no negative marking and rewards a full attempt. Give the second half to full-length mock tests taken at the same time of day as your slot, followed by a careful review of every wrong answer. For general awareness, a single daily current affairs source plus a static general knowledge booklet covers most of what the paper asks. English improves fastest through daily reading and a fixed set of grammar rules rather than memorising word lists. The candidates who convert this exam are rarely the ones who studied the most. They are the ones who made the fewest careless errors in Session II.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the last date to apply for SSC MTS 2026?**
The last date to apply for SSC MTS 2026 is 31 July 2026, with fee payment also closing on the same day at 11:00 PM. The notification was released on 30 June 2026.

**How many vacancies are there in SSC MTS 2026?**
SSC MTS 2026 has 7,948 vacancies, split into roughly 6,810 Multi-Tasking Staff posts and 1,138 Havaldar posts in CBIC and CBN, per the SSC MTS 2026 notification.

**Is there negative marking in SSC MTS 2026?**
Yes, but only in Session II. General awareness and English carry a penalty of 1 mark per wrong answer, while Session I (maths and reasoning) has no negative marking, so you can attempt every question there.

**What is the in-hand salary of SSC MTS in 2026?**
A Level 1 MTS recruit takes home about Rs 33,000 a month in a metro (X city) at the 60 percent dearness allowance effective 1 January 2026, and about Rs 29,000 in a Z-class city, after standard deductions.

**What is the qualification needed for SSC MTS?**
A Class 10 (Matriculation) pass from a recognised board is the only qualification needed for SSC MTS. There is no minimum percentage and no upper degree requirement.

**Who has to appear for the PET and PST in SSC MTS?**
Only Havaldar applicants appear for the Physical Efficiency Test and Physical Standard Test. Multi-Tasking Staff posts have no physical test, and the Havaldar PET and PST are qualifying rather than merit-deciding.

**How is the SSC MTS age limit calculated?**
Age is reckoned as on 1 August 2026. Most MTS posts need 18 to 25 years, while Havaldar and some MTS posts allow 18 to 27 years, with category relaxations of 3 years for OBC, 5 years for SC and ST, and up to 15 years for PwBD.

**What is the difference between MTS and Havaldar?**
MTS involves office and support duties across central government departments at Pay Level 1, while Havaldar is a field role in customs (CBIC) and narcotics control (CBN) at the same pay level, with an added physical test at selection.
