The Staff Selection Commission published its examination calendar for 2026-27 on 8 January 2026, covering notification months, application closing dates and tentative examination windows for every major SSC recruitment.

Every site reproduces that table. Almost none mentions the thing that matters most about it: the calendar is tentative, and this year it moved.

I can show you by how much, because we track the actual dates on individual exam pages and they can be compared against what the calendar promised.

## What the calendar said

| Exam | Notification | Exam window |
|---|---|---|
| CGL 2026 | March 2026 | May to June 2026 |
| JE 2026 | March 2026 | Paper 1 alongside CGL |
| CHSL 2026 | April 2026 | July to September 2026 |
| Stenographer Grade C and D | April 2026 | August to September 2026 |
| MTS and Havaldar 2026 | Process from June 2026 | September to November 2026 |
| GD Constable 2027 | Process from September 2026 | January to March 2027 |

The calendar runs through to January 2027. SSC releases more than 80,000 vacancies a year across these examinations, spanning Class 10, Class 12 and graduate eligibility, which is why the calendar is the single most consulted SSC document outside the notifications themselves.

## What actually happened, exam by exam

Here is the comparison nobody publishes.

**SSC CGL 2026.** The calendar said notification in March and examinations in May to June. The notification was actually released on 21 May 2026, and SSC then set Tier 1 for 30 September to 30 October 2026 in an exam notice dated 12 September. That is roughly a two month slip on the notification and a four month slip on the examination.

**SSC CHSL 2026.** The calendar said notification in April and a Tier 1 window from July to September. The notification came on 30 April 2026 and Tier 1 ran across July to September. That is close to the calendar, essentially on schedule.

So the slip is not uniform. One flagship examination moved by roughly a quarter, while another landed where it was supposed to. That variation is the practically useful finding, and it means you cannot apply a blanket correction to the calendar and call it a plan.

## Why calendars slip

Understanding the causes helps you judge which entries are more likely to move.

Vacancy confirmation is the most common driver. SSC recruits on behalf of participating ministries and departments, and a notification cannot issue until those departments have confirmed their requirements. A department that is slow to report holds the whole notification.

Examination logistics matter at this scale. Conducting a computer-based test for millions of candidates across weeks requires centre capacity, and centre availability interacts with every other examination running in the same period, including state recruitments and university examinations.

Litigation affects SSC recruitment regularly. Court orders on eligibility, reservation, result processing or conduct of a previous cycle can pause or reschedule an examination at short notice.

Administrative decisions, including changes to the examination pattern, can require a rescheduled notification. The sectional timing change introduced in CGL 2026 is an example of a substantive pattern change landing in a cycle.

None of these are failures. They are the normal friction of running recruitment at this scale, and the calendar is published as tentative precisely because SSC knows they occur.

## How to use the calendar properly

The calendar is a planning instrument, not a schedule. Used correctly it is genuinely valuable.

Use it for sequencing rather than for dates. Knowing that CGL and JE notifications land in the same window, and that MTS follows in the middle of the year, lets you plan which examinations you will attempt and how their preparation overlaps. That sequencing holds even when individual dates move.

Use it to identify collisions. Where two examinations you want to sit have overlapping windows, you have advance warning to think about how you will handle both, and that warning survives a slip because both entries tend to move together.

Use it to set a preparation floor rather than a peak. If the calendar says an examination is in May, being ready in May is correct even if it lands in August, because readiness that arrives early costs nothing while readiness that arrives late costs the attempt.

Do not use it to book travel, plan leave from work, or schedule anything that carries a cancellation cost. Only the admit card does that.

Do not treat a passed calendar date as evidence that an examination has been abandoned. A notification arriving two months after its calendar month is ordinary.

## The examinations still ahead

Several entries on this calendar are still in front of candidates as of August 2026.

MTS and Havaldar 2026 has its examination window from September to November 2026. This is the largest SSC recruitment by candidate volume, open at Class 10 level, and it draws an enormous applicant pool.

Stenographer Grade C and D was scheduled for August to September 2026, a window that has now passed.

GD Constable 2027 begins its process from September 2026, which is next month, with the computer-based examination scheduled for January to March 2027. This is the largest recruitment on the calendar by vacancy count in most cycles, filling constable posts across the central armed police forces, and candidates targeting it should start watching for the notification several months before the calendar month, not in it.

For each of these, the calendar month is where to start watching, not where to expect the event.

## What each examination on the calendar actually recruits for

The calendar lists codes and dates. What it does not tell a candidate deciding where to spend a year is what each examination leads to.

**Combined Graduate Level** recruits graduates into Group B and Group C posts across central ministries. It is the flagship: Assistant Section Officer, Inspector in Income Tax and in Central Excise and GST, Assistant Audit Officer, Assistant Enforcement Officer, Sub Inspector in the CBI, Junior Statistical Officer and Tax Assistant among others. Pay levels run from 4 to 8, so the range within a single examination is wide.

**Combined Higher Secondary Level** recruits at Class 12 level into Lower Division Clerk and Junior Secretariat Assistant, Data Entry Operator, and Postal Assistant and Sorting Assistant. Pay levels 2 and 4. It carries a typing or data entry skill test that is qualifying but eliminating.

**Multi Tasking Staff and Havaldar** recruits at Class 10 level, making it the most widely eligible examination SSC runs and the one with the largest candidate pool. Havaldar posts in CBIC and CBN add a physical standard and physical efficiency test.

**Junior Engineer** recruits diploma and degree holders in Civil, Mechanical and Electrical engineering into central engineering departments at pay level 6.

**Stenographer Grade C and D** recruits at Class 12 level with a shorthand skill test, which is a genuinely specialised requirement that narrows the field considerably compared with other Class 12 examinations.

**GD Constable** recruits at Class 10 level into the central armed police forces, with physical standards, a physical efficiency test and a medical examination alongside the written paper.

**Selection Post** runs separately and recruits to specific posts across departments at varying eligibility levels, with phases through the year.

Reading the calendar alongside this list is what turns it from a table of dates into a plan.

## The overlap that makes multiple attempts sensible

Candidates frequently ask which SSC examination to target, and the framing is usually wrong because it assumes a choice is necessary.

The written syllabus across CGL, CHSL and MTS covers the same four areas: general intelligence and reasoning, general awareness, quantitative aptitude and English. What differs is depth and the level of the questions, not the subject matter.

A graduate preparing seriously for CGL is substantially prepared for CHSL and comfortably prepared for MTS. The additional cost of sitting all three is the application fee and the examination days.

What differs meaningfully is the skill test component. CHSL requires typing or data entry speed, Stenographer requires shorthand, and GD Constable requires physical standards. Those are genuine additional requirements that need their own preparation and cannot be improvised.

The practical strategy for most graduates is to prepare the shared foundation, sit every examination in the portfolio they are eligible for, and add typing practice because it unlocks CHSL and several Selection Post positions at low cost.

Candidates who decline lower-level examinations because the pay is lower should weigh a real post at level 2 against a hypothetical one at level 7. Internal promotion routes exist, departmental examinations accelerate them, and a candidate inside the system has options a candidate outside it does not.

## What to watch instead of the calendar

Once a notification issues, the calendar stops being the relevant document and several others take over.

The notification itself governs eligibility, the application window, the fee and the examination scheme. It supersedes anything the calendar implied.

Corrigenda are issued during cycles and they amend the notification. SSC publishes them without individual notice, and they have changed dates, vacancy counts and occasionally eligibility wording in past cycles.

The city intimation slip tells you your allotted city several days before your batch, and it carries nothing else.

The admit card is the only document that states your date, shift, centre and reporting time. Everything else is planning.

Check ssc.gov.in directly rather than relying on aggregator notification. SSC publishes and does not individually notify, and aggregators report with a lag and occasionally with errors.

## Planning a year around SSC examinations

Given how the calendar works, a sensible approach to the year looks different from waiting for dates.

Decide which examinations you are eligible for and want to attempt, using the calendar for sequencing. A graduate is eligible for CGL, CHSL, MTS and several others, and the syllabus overlap across them is substantial.

Build the shared foundation continuously. General awareness, quantitative aptitude, reasoning and English appear across the SSC portfolio at different depths, so work on them serves every examination you sit rather than one.

Sit everything you are eligible for. The preparation is shared, the marginal cost of an additional application is a fee and a day, and candidates who hold out for a single examination often spend years doing it. A graduate skipping CHSL because CGL pays better is declining a real chance at a government post for a hypothetical one.

Treat each notification as the trigger for cycle-specific work: the exact pattern, any changes from the previous year, and the practical logistics.

Keep your One Time Registration current so that a notification arriving early does not catch you assembling documents.

## Building a twelve month plan from a tentative calendar

Here is how to turn the calendar into something you can act on, accepting that individual dates will move.

Start by listing the examinations you are eligible for. Eligibility is a fact about your qualification and age, and it does not move with the calendar. A graduate under 27 is eligible for most of the portfolio; a Class 12 candidate for a smaller set.

Group them by the skill requirements they add. CGL and JE need only the written preparation. CHSL adds typing. Stenographer adds shorthand. GD Constable adds physical standards. Those additions take months, so decide early which you are willing to acquire.

Work backwards from the earliest calendar entry you are targeting, then add a buffer in the wrong direction. If the calendar says May, plan to be ready in April rather than assuming August. Early readiness is free; late readiness is not.

Treat the shared foundation as continuous rather than campaign-based. General awareness in particular rewards daily accumulation across a year and punishes compression, which means it should be running regardless of which notification is currently open.

Reserve intensity for the weeks after a notification issues, when the pattern, the vacancy position and the actual dates are known.

Review the plan when notifications land rather than when calendar months pass. A notification changes real facts; a calendar month passing changes nothing.

## Common mistakes candidates make with the calendar

Treating tentative dates as fixed, then feeling misled when they move. The document says tentative and it means it.

Concluding an examination has been cancelled because its calendar month passed without a notification. A one to two month lag is ordinary.

Planning peak preparation for the calendar month rather than being ready by it. Peaking for a date that then moves by three months is how candidates arrive stale.

Booking anything cancellable around calendar dates. Only the admit card is authoritative on when and where you sit.

Waiting for a single examination while declining others in the portfolio. The preparation is shared and the marginal cost of another attempt is small.

Relying on aggregator sites for notification alerts. SSC publishes on its own site without individual notice, and aggregators lag and occasionally err.

Ignoring skill test requirements until after a written result. Typing, shorthand and physical standards take months and cannot be acquired in the gap.

Assuming the pattern carries over from last year. SSC changed CGL Tier 1 to sectional timing in this cycle, which materially altered attempt strategy for anyone who had prepared on the old format.

## Frequently asked questions

**When was the SSC calendar 2026-27 released?**

On 8 January 2026, on the official SSC website. It covers notification months, application closing dates and tentative examination windows for CGL, CHSL, MTS, JE, CPO, Stenographer, GD Constable and Selection Post examinations, running through to January 2027.

**Are SSC calendar dates guaranteed?**

No. The calendar is explicitly tentative and dates move. This cycle, CGL 2026 was scheduled for a March notification with May to June examinations and actually saw a 21 May notification with Tier 1 running from 30 September to 30 October 2026, roughly a three month slip on the examination. CHSL by contrast ran close to its calendar entry.

**Why do SSC exam dates get delayed?**

Most often because participating departments have not confirmed vacancies, since a notification cannot issue until they do. Examination logistics at this scale, litigation affecting eligibility or a previous cycle, and administrative changes to the examination pattern also cause rescheduling.

**Which SSC exams are still ahead in 2026?**

CGL Tier 1 from 30 September to 30 October 2026, MTS and Havaldar with an examination window running to November 2026, and GD Constable 2027, which begins its process from September 2026 with the computer-based examination from January to March 2027.

**When will SSC GD Constable 2027 be notified?**

The calendar places the start of the process in September 2026, with the computer-based examination from January to March 2027. Candidates targeting it should watch ssc.gov.in from September rather than waiting until closer to the examination, since the application window typically runs about a month from notification.

**How many vacancies does SSC release each year?**

More than 80,000 across its examinations, spanning Class 10, Class 12 and graduate eligibility levels. That scale is why the calendar is the most consulted SSC document outside the notifications themselves.

**Should I plan travel around calendar dates?**

No. Only the admit card states your examination date, shift, centre and reporting time. The calendar is for sequencing your preparation and identifying collisions between examinations, not for anything that carries a cancellation cost.

**What if a calendar month passes with no notification?**

That is ordinary rather than a signal the examination has been dropped. A notification arriving one to two months after its calendar month has been common. Keep watching ssc.gov.in rather than concluding a cycle has been abandoned.

**Which SSC exam should I prepare for first?**

Prepare the shared foundation rather than a single examination. General awareness, quantitative aptitude, reasoning and English recur across the SSC portfolio at different depths, so the work transfers. Then sit every examination you are eligible for, because the marginal cost of an additional application is small and holding out for one examination costs years.

**Where do I download the official SSC calendar?**

From ssc.gov.in, where SSC publishes the calendar PDF. Aggregator reproductions are usually accurate but they are secondary, and the official PDF is what governs where they disagree.

**Does the SSC calendar cover Selection Post exams?**

The calendar includes Selection Post phases alongside the main examinations. Selection Post recruits to specific positions across departments at varying eligibility levels, from Class 10 through graduate, and it runs in phases through the year rather than as a single examination. It is worth watching because the eligibility varies post by post, so a candidate ineligible for one phase may qualify for the next.

**Is there a separate calendar for SSC CPO?**

CPO appears in the same 2026-27 calendar as the other examinations. It recruits Sub Inspector posts in Delhi Police and the central armed police forces, and it carries physical standards and a physical efficiency test alongside the written papers, so candidates targeting it need physical preparation running in parallel with the written work.

**How far in advance does SSC release the calendar?**

SSC publishes the tentative calendar ahead of the cycle it covers, and the 2026-27 calendar was released on 8 January 2026 running through to January 2027. That gives roughly a year of advance sequencing information, which is its genuine value even though individual dates move within it.

**Can I apply for two SSC exams at the same time?**

Yes. The examinations have separate notifications, separate applications and separate fees, and there is no restriction on applying to multiple. Where examination windows collide, SSC generally schedules around its own conflicts, but you should check dates once admit cards issue rather than assuming no clash.

## Sources

- Staff Selection Commission: https://ssc.gov.in

The calendar, notifications and corrigenda all appear there first. Where this article and an SSC document differ, the SSC document governs, and where the calendar and a notification differ, the notification governs.

One closing observation. The frustration candidates feel about calendar slippage comes largely from treating a tentative planning document as a promise. Read as what it is, an advance indication of sequence and rough timing, it does its job well. Read as a schedule, it will disappoint you every year.

Pay levels run from 4 to 8, so the range within a single examination is wide.

**Combined Higher Secondary Level** recruits at Class 12 level into Lower Division Clerk and Junior Secretariat Assistant, Data Entry Operator, and Postal Assistant and Sorting Assistant. Pay levels 2 and 4. It carries a typing or data entry skill test that is qualifying but eliminating.

**Multi Tasking Staff and Havaldar** recruits at Class 10 level, making it the most widely eligible examination SSC runs and the one with the largest candidate pool. Havaldar posts in CBIC and CBN add a physical standard and physical efficiency test.

**Junior Engineer** recruits diploma and degree holders in Civil, Mechanical and Electrical engineering into central engineering departments at pay level 6.

**Stenographer Grade C and D** recruits at Class 12 level with a shorthand skill test, which is a genuinely specialised requirement that narrows the field considerably compared with other Class 12 examinations.

**GD Constable** recruits at Class 10 level into the central armed police forces, with physical standards, a physical efficiency test and a medical examination alongside the written paper.

**Selection Post** runs separately and recruits to specific posts across departments at varying eligibility levels, with phases through the year.

Reading the calendar alongside this list is what turns it from a table of dates into a plan.

## The overlap that makes multiple attempts sensible

Candidates frequently ask which SSC examination to target, and the framing is usually wrong because it assumes a choice is necessary.

The written syllabus across CGL, CHSL and MTS covers the same four areas: general intelligence and reasoning, general awareness, quantitative aptitude and English. What differs is depth and the level of the questions, not the subject matter.

A graduate preparing seriously for CGL is substantially prepared for CHSL and comfortably prepared for MTS. The additional cost of sitting all three is the application fee and the examination days.

What differs meaningfully is the skill test component. CHSL requires typing or data entry speed, Stenographer requires shorthand, and GD Constable requires physical standards. Those are genuine additional requirements that need their own preparation and cannot be improvised.

The practical strategy for most graduates is to prepare the shared foundation, sit every examination in the portfolio they are eligible for, and add typing practice because it unlocks CHSL and several Selection Post positions at low cost.

Candidates who decline lower-level examinations because the pay is lower should weigh a real post at level 2 against a hypothetical one at level 7. Internal promotion routes exist, departmental examinations accelerate them, and a candidate inside the system has options a candidate outside it does not.

## What to watch instead of the calendar

Once a notification issues, the calendar stops being the relevant document and several others take over.

The notification itself governs eligibility, the application window, the fee and the examination scheme. It supersedes anything the calendar implied.

Corrigenda are issued during cycles and they amend the notification. SSC publishes them without individual notice, and they have changed dates, vacancy counts and occasionally eligibility wording in past cycles.

The city intimation slip tells you your allotted city several days before your batch, and it carries nothing else.

The admit card is the only document that states your date, shift, centre and reporting time. Everything else is planning.

Check ssc.gov.in directly rather than relying on aggregator notification. SSC publishes and does not individually notify, and aggregators report with a lag and occasionally with errors.

## Planning a year around SSC examinations

Given how the calendar works, a sensible approach to the year looks different from waiting for dates.

Decide which examinations you are eligible for and want to attempt, using the calendar for sequencing. A graduate is eligible for CGL, CHSL, MTS and several others, and the syllabus overlap across them is substantial.

Build the shared foundation continuously. General awareness, quantitative aptitude, reasoning and English appear across the SSC portfolio at different depths, so work on them serves every examination you sit rather than one.

Sit everything you are eligible for. The preparation is shared, the marginal cost of an additional application is a fee and a day, and candidates who hold out for a single examination often spend years doing it. A graduate skipping CHSL because CGL pays better is declining a real chance at a government post for a hypothetical one.

Treat each notification as the trigger for cycle-specific work: the exact pattern, any changes from the previous year, and the practical logistics.

Keep your One Time Registration current so that a notification arriving early does not catch you assembling documents.

## Building a twelve month plan from a tentative calendar

Here is how to turn the calendar into something you can act on, accepting that individual dates will move.

Start by listing the examinations you are eligible for. Eligibility is a fact about your qualification and age, and it does not move with the calendar. A graduate under 27 is eligible for most of the portfolio; a Class 12 candidate for a smaller set.

Group them by the skill requirements they add. CGL and JE need only the written preparation. CHSL adds typing. Stenographer adds shorthand. GD Constable adds physical standards. Those additions take months, so decide early which you are willing to acquire.

Work backwards from the earliest calendar entry you are targeting, then add a buffer in the wrong direction. If the calendar says May, plan to be ready in April rather than assuming August. Early readiness is free; late readiness is not.

Treat the shared foundation as continuous rather than campaign-based. General awareness in particular rewards daily accumulation across a year and punishes compression, which means it should be running regardless of which notification is currently open.

Reserve intensity for the weeks after a notification issues, when the pattern, the vacancy position and the actual dates are known.

Review the plan when notifications land rather than when calendar months pass. A notification changes real facts; a calendar month passing changes nothing.

## Common mistakes candidates make with the calendar

Treating tentative dates as fixed, then feeling misled when they move. The document says tentative and it means it.

Concluding an examination has been cancelled because its calendar month passed without a notification. A one to two month lag is ordinary.

Planning peak preparation for the calendar month rather than being ready by it. Peaking for a date that then moves by three months is how candidates arrive stale.

Booking anything cancellable around calendar dates. Only the admit card is authoritative on when and where you sit.

Waiting for a single examination while declining others in the portfolio. The preparation is shared and the marginal cost of another attempt is small.

Relying on aggregator sites for notification alerts. SSC publishes on its own site without individual notice, and aggregators lag and occasionally err.

Ignoring skill test requirements until after a written result. Typing, shorthand and physical standards take months and cannot be acquired in the gap.

Assuming the pattern carries over from last year. SSC changed CGL Tier 1 to sectional timing in this cycle, which materially altered attempt strategy for anyone who had prepared on the old format.

## Frequently asked questions

**When was the SSC calendar 2026-27 released?**

On 8 January 2026, on the official SSC website. It covers notification months, application closing dates and tentative examination windows for CGL, CHSL, MTS, JE, CPO, Stenographer, GD Constable and Selection Post examinations, running through to January 2027.

**Are SSC calendar dates guaranteed?**

No. The calendar is explicitly tentative and dates move. This cycle, CGL 2026 was scheduled for a March notification with May to June examinations and actually saw a 21 May notification with Tier 1 running from 30 September to 30 October 2026, roughly a three month slip on the examination. CHSL by contrast ran close to its calendar entry.

**Why do SSC exam dates get delayed?**

Most often because participating departments have not confirmed vacancies, since a notification cannot issue until they do. Examination logistics at this scale, litigation affecting eligibility or a previous cycle, and administrative changes to the examination pattern also cause rescheduling.

**Which SSC exams are still ahead in 2026?**

CGL Tier 1 from 30 September to 30 October 2026, MTS and Havaldar with an examination window running to November 2026, and GD Constable 2027, which begins its process from September 2026 with the computer-based examination from January to March 2027.

**When will SSC GD Constable 2027 be notified?**

The calendar places the start of the process in September 2026, with the computer-based examination from January to March 2027. Candidates targeting it should watch ssc.gov.in from September rather than waiting until closer to the examination, since the application window typically runs about a month from notification.

**How many vacancies does SSC release each year?**

More than 80,000 across its examinations, spanning Class 10, Class 12 and graduate eligibility levels. That scale is why the calendar is the most consulted SSC document outside the notifications themselves.

**Should I plan travel around calendar dates?**

No. Only the admit card states your examination date, shift, centre and reporting time. The calendar is for sequencing your preparation and identifying collisions between examinations, not for anything that carries a cancellation cost.

**What if a calendar month passes with no notification?**

That is ordinary rather than a signal the examination has been dropped. A notification arriving one to two months after its calendar month has been common. Keep watching ssc.gov.in rather than concluding a cycle has been abandoned.

**Which SSC exam should I prepare for first?**

Prepare the shared foundation rather than a single examination. General awareness, quantitative aptitude, reasoning and English recur across the SSC portfolio at different depths, so the work transfers. Then sit every examination you are eligible for, because the marginal cost of an additional application is small and holding out for one examination costs years.

**Where do I download the official SSC calendar?**

From ssc.gov.in, where SSC publishes the calendar PDF. Aggregator reproductions are usually accurate but they are secondary, and the official PDF is what governs where they disagree.

**Does the SSC calendar cover Selection Post exams?**

The calendar includes Selection Post phases alongside the main examinations. Selection Post recruits to specific positions across departments at varying eligibility levels, from Class 10 through graduate, and it runs in phases through the year rather than as a single examination. It is worth watching because the eligibility varies post by post, so a candidate ineligible for one phase may qualify for the next.

**Is there a separate calendar for SSC CPO?**

CPO appears in the same 2026-27 calendar as the other examinations. It recruits Sub Inspector posts in Delhi Police and the central armed police forces, and it carries physical standards and a physical efficiency test alongside the written papers, so candidates targeting it need physical preparation running in parallel with the written work.

**How far in advance does SSC release the calendar?**

SSC publishes the tentative calendar ahead of the cycle it covers, and the 2026-27 calendar was released on 8 January 2026 running through to January 2027. That gives roughly a year of advance sequencing information, which is its genuine value even though individual dates move within it.

**Can I apply for two SSC exams at the same time?**

Yes. The examinations have separate notifications, separate applications and separate fees, and there is no restriction on applying to multiple. Where examination windows collide, SSC generally schedules around its own conflicts, but you should check dates once admit cards issue rather than assuming no clash.
